paragraphs.text: The labors of endurance are good, and the fruit that follows those labors is the finest of all, for good labors bear glorious fruit. Labors give birth to virtues. To labors belongs the proclamation of the fast. By labors the splendid campaign of martyrdom is carried to victory. The prize for labors is the kingdom of heaven. With these holy labors we have completed this all-virtuous week. The first contest has run to its end, and the prize of piety shines out. Today, brothers, is the day on which Adam was formed, the day on which he came into being in the image of God. Yesterday my voice would not obey me, so today, on the very day on which Adam was formed, I must take up again the discourse on his formation. God formed him on this day, and on this day he forms him anew.

What then? Shall we take up the subject we promised? When God made the world, he adorned the heaven with sun and moon and stars. In the same way he embroidered the earth, girding it with rivers and springs and crowning it with flowers and plants. He walled off the sea and clothed this world in all its beauty, as I have often said before. Then he fashioned and formed a master for this world, appointed by his own hand. But he does not form him as he formed the others. The four-footed creatures, the wild beasts and the cattle he brought forth from the earth by a word of command alone: "Let the earth bring forth four-footed creatures, creeping things and wild beasts." The servants are summoned by a word, but the creature that bears the divine image is shaped by a hand. It is not that God has a hand or any such limb. Rather, Scripture wishes to show the dignity of what is being formed, and so it brings in the hand of God at work. For we get the menial tasks done by giving orders, but the things we cherish we take up with our own hands. That is why Scripture says, "And God took dust from the earth." He took dust: not a clod, not the coarsest earth, but the finest dust. See how the hope of the resurrection was planted from the very beginning! Man was going to be dissolved into dust, as it is said: "And you brought me down into the dust of death." So that no one who saw the dust in the tombs would give up hope for human beings, God planted the hope of the resurrection in the act of creation itself. That is why it says, God took dust from the earth. There it is dust, and here it is dust. The one was transformed by the power of the craftsman, and the other is changed by the wisdom of the Creator. He took dust and formed him.

You have learned where he took it from and what he formed. But how he transformed it you have not been told. Scripture spoke of the formation but hid the manner, so that you might learn not to pry into God's work of creation. And if you are not permitted to pry into God's creation, you ought much less to meddle with God's begetting. Next: when God made the four-footed creatures, he brought forth their souls together with their bodies. But in forming man he first prepares the instrument of the body, and only then does he create the soul and place it within. Why? To show in this too the preeminence of man. When the other animals and the cattle are dissolved by death, the soul vanishes together with the body. So Scripture speaks of their origin as coming from the place where the whole of them would vanish again. God, then, in forming man, takes the body from the earth, but the soul he breathes in.

Wait a little, and I will set before you, as far as I can, the meaning of this breathing. From the very beginning God sketches the hope of the resurrection in this too. He forms the body first. Man first received a lifeless image, and only then received the living activity of the soul. First he was shown dead, then alive. First God formed a dead body, which is what man was going to end in. Then, when he had finished the dead body, he gave it its living stamp. He does not make the soul first, so that it would not be an eyewitness of what was taking place. He does not let the soul be present at the creation, so that it could not boast of being God's fellow worker. And not only so that it could not boast, but so that it could not even see how the work was done. God does this even now. He forms each of us in the womb, and he has allowed no one to see how he forms us. We are sown and we are formed. Nature runs its course, but no one grasps how the forming is done. O the wonder of it! A temple is built within a temple, a house is constructed within a house, and the outer house does not even perceive it.

So he makes man after the pattern of a lifeless image. Then Scripture says, "God breathed into the face of Adam the breath of life, and man became a living soul." Many have supposed that his breath was the soul, and that the soul was imparted to the body from the very substance of God. But this view is full not only of great folly but of absurdity. If the soul were from the substance of God, it should not be wise in one person and foolish and senseless in another, nor righteous in this one and unrighteous in that one. The substance of God is not divided or altered; it is unchangeable. "For I am," he says, "and I have not changed." Further, brothers, we not only find souls that go astray, which proves that they are not of the divine substance. We also find them subject to judgment. For the Savior says, "Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna." If, then, the soul came from his own substance, God would be judging himself.

We must therefore see what the breathing means. In God's case, the breathing is the working of the Holy Spirit. The Savior breathed on the faces of the apostles and said, "Receive the Holy Spirit." In the same way the divine breathing, spoken of in human terms, is the Holy Spirit who is to be worshiped. This Spirit went forth, yet it did not itself become the soul; it created the soul. It was not itself changed into a soul; it fashioned a soul. For the Holy Spirit is Creator. It shares in creating the body and in creating the soul. Father, Son and Holy Spirit create the creature by the divine power. And do not think that the Father contributed one part, the Son another and the Holy Spirit another. What I mean is this: even when the Father makes something, the work belongs to the Son and the achievement to the Spirit. And even when the Son creates, the creation belongs to the Father, and the creation belongs to the Holy Spirit.

If anyone refuses to believe this and holds that the Holy Spirit had no share in our creation, let him be refuted from the sacred mysteries. If we were not created by the Trinity, how is the rite of initiation also inscribed with the name of the Holy Spirit? How is our creation renewed in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit? When we were created, was there no need of the Spirit, yet when we are renewed, the Spirit is brought in? Therefore the Holy Spirit is Creator, whether its enemies like it or not. And David bears witness to the creative power of the Spirit. Speaking of how human beings are made, he says: "All things wait for you, Lord, to give them their food in due season. When you give it, they will gather it; when you open your hand, all things will be filled with goodness." These words show his bountiful provision. Then what follows? "But when you turn away your face, they will be troubled. You will take away their spirit, and they will fail and return to their dust. You will send forth your Spirit, and they will be created."

So the Holy Spirit is Founder and Creator. And notice how precise the words are. When he speaks of our soul, he says, "You will take away their spirit, and they will fail and return to their dust." But when he speaks of the Holy Spirit, he says, "You will send forth your Spirit, and they will be created." If the heretics dare to set themselves against this truth, another testimony will drive them back, one that proclaims the creative power of the Holy Spirit. For something greater than all creation, greater than heaven and earth and sea, turns out to be the work of the Holy Spirit. The all-holy body of Christ, which we worship, through which heaven and earth and the whole world are renewed and all humankind is saved, is the work of the Holy Spirit. When the holy Virgin was perplexed at the strange birth announced to her, she said, "How will this be for me, since I do not know a man?" And the angel says to her, "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you." Some have thought that "Holy Spirit" here means the Spirit himself, and "power of the Most High" means the Son. But one must understand that the angel called the same one both Holy Spirit and power of the Most High. The Son is called the power of the Most High, for Christ is the power of God, and in the same way the Holy Spirit is also called power. Thus the Lord says to the apostles, "Stay in Jerusalem until you are clothed with power from on high." And before this, brothers, the angel speaks to Joseph and says, "Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife. For what has been made in her" (he does not say "begotten," so that you would not think the divine and undefiled nature a created thing) "is from the Holy Spirit." If, then, the Holy Spirit created the body of Christ, show me a difference between one act of creation and the other. But take care that you are not put to shame by ascribing the earthly image to the Father and the heavenly one to the Spirit. For if, as you claim, the Spirit had no share in the creation when Adam was created, then the Father and the Son will turn out to have created the earthly man, and the Spirit the heavenly one. "He breathed into his face, and man became a living soul."

Now pay close attention. When Adam was formed, when he was fashioned, when he received his own stamp, the woman had not yet been formed. But what does God do? He did not want Adam's soul to be present at the creation of the body, and in the same way he allowed no mortal eye to be present at the creation of the woman. That is why, when he was about to form the woman, he cast sleep upon Adam, so that Adam would not be there to pry into God's work. "And he cast a trance upon him" (that is, sleep) "and he slept. And he took one of his ribs." He who had bound also loosed. He borrows from what he is working on; he takes from what he is making. "He took one of his ribs and filled up flesh in its place." Where he filled it up from, words cannot tell; but power is never at a loss. "And he built the rib which he had taken into a woman." How, again, did he build it? How was a rib-bone transformed into an eye? How was it shaped into hands? How was it stretched out into sinews? How did it take on the color of a liver? How was it remodeled into the varied organs within? How was a tongue set in place? How were lips turned as on a lathe? How were nostrils carved? How were ears spread out? How did hair blossom? Where did nails grow from? How does the blood run through the body? Explain your own creation. And if you cannot tell, then muzzle your slander against the Only-Begotten. God cast a trance upon Adam, and he slept. And he takes a rib and creates a woman.

See the all-wise wisdom here. From one he forms two, so that from the two he may make one again through union. From Adam he made the woman: from the one he made two. Then the same God makes the one from the two, for what is born of woman and man he brings to completion as one body. The words are human, but the meaning is divine. Explain how she was built, and you will not discover how the rib was built. How did he form the one and build the other? Is forming from earth the same thing as building from a rib? God formed Adam from earth. He created Eve from a rib. He makes Cain and Abel and the rest of humankind through union. So the others are begotten, the one is formed, and the other is built. The names are not equal. Was the substance divided, then? Not at all. I say this at the right moment, since the heretics say that the begotten and the unbegotten are not alike, but that the realities are as far apart as the names are different. Then show me the difference between Adam and those born from him. Adam is both originate and unbegotten: originate, in that he came into being; unbegotten, in that he was not begotten. He came into being and was formed, but was not begotten. The woman was neither begotten nor formed. Take up the words once more and fix their meaning. Adam was formed and not begotten. The woman was built: she was neither formed from earth nor born from a womb, as Cain was. And the rest were neither formed nor built, but begotten. The meanings of these terms differ greatly, then: to be formed is one thing, to be built another, to be begotten another. So show me a difference of substance between Adam and Eve and their offspring. And if they are distinguished by their names but not by their substance, what is so surprising? You may keep turning the names around, but though they differ in sound, they agree in truth.

Where did you get this "begotten" versus "unbegotten"? You have rejected the names Father and Son. You have made yourself wiser than the Holy Spirit in choosing names. Was God not more trustworthy than you? Could he not have found this clever idea himself before you invented it? Could he not have said, "Baptize them in the name of the Unbegotten and the Begotten"? But let the battle against the heretics and the contest for true religion be saved for another occasion. Let us return to our subject: He cast sleep upon Adam, and then he took the rib.

From this rib, then, the occasion of the transgression was to come forth, for it was woman who brought death upon Adam. So the Savior, wishing to heal the wound, sets side against rib: on the cross he gave over his side to the spear, so that salvation might blossom from the very place where the wound had come from. Blood and water came out. Understand the mystery, honor the one who ordered it, and see the wonder. Adam's rib was taken from him after he had fallen asleep; it was not taken while Adam was awake. In the same way the Savior's side was not pierced while he was awake in the body. Only after his body had fallen asleep did he give his side to the soldier.

Now pay close attention. When the Savior was fulfilling the divine plan on the cross, he endured everything else while he was still in the flesh and visible, as befits the human condition. For suffering does not touch God. Suffering does not dishonor God. Suffering does not diminish God, unless he is somehow lower even than our souls. He himself gives this promise to our souls when he says, "Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul." How, then, could he himself share in the sufferings of the body? Does the soul not die, while the one who created souls dies? Having endured everything that belonged to his plan as a man, at its end he wished to show the sovereignty of that plan: that its authority acts with full command and does not bow to the laws of nature. So he says on the cross, "It is finished. Father, into your hands I commit my spirit." With his voice he dissolved nature; by his word he had fitted together its frame. For he is the one who says, "I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again." So he gave up his spirit in human fashion and died, or rather, by his dying he put death to death. The soldiers could not believe how quickly his release had come, and they realized that to give up one's soul at a bare word is beyond human nature. So they came to test whether he was alive. And they found him truly dead in body, but alive in power. The one they had killed as a man they confessed after the cross to be the Son of God. For when the soldier opened his side with a spear, blood and water came out, which is not the way of a dead man. Blood never springs from a dead man. But when the mystical blood sprang forth, that side opened a fountain of salvation, to answer the rib that had opened the way to lawlessness. Then the centurion standing by the cross says, "Truly this was the Son of God." You denied him while he lived, and now that he is dead you proclaim him?

So pay close attention to what is being said. God cast sleep upon Adam and then drew out the rib. In the same way, when the Savior had undergone in his body the sleep that is common to all, his side was pierced. For both then, after the sleep, and now, after the falling asleep, the soldiers saw blood and proclaimed him Son of God. But the heretics, even when they see a miracle, call him a creature. And why, brothers, did his side meet the spear? Everything that stood against Adam had to be undone in the figure of the cross. When God cast Adam out of paradise, he set around it the flaming sword to keep him from entering paradise, and the sword was turning. Now anything that turns does not stop until it strikes against something in its way. You know from experience, brothers, what I mean: anything that turns does not stop in its course unless it strikes something. No one, then, could withstand the fiery sword. So in his plan of the cross he set his side against the sword's form, so that the spiritual sword might strike his side by means of the visible spear, cease at last from its threat, and no longer shut people out of paradise. The Lord, then, received the sword in his side, and at once the door of paradise was opened. Healing sprang from a side for the one who had been wounded through a rib. First he led him out of paradise, and at the end he led the same man into the kingdom. He disciplined him, but he showed him mercy. He cast him out, but he did not destroy him. He turned him away, but he did not drive him off for good.

But I know it is time to give way to the liturgy. For all things are possible with God, so he can put into our minds an understanding of what remains, and can let the hearers see from a part the force of the whole discourse. For "give a wise man an occasion, and he will be wiser still." Let us give thanks to God, then: we lost one paradise, and he has planted countless paradises throughout the whole world. Let us give thanks to God: having lost paradise through transgression, we have been called to the kingdom of heaven, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.
